passage: Mateo was locking up the Madrid co-working office when he saw Fatima's corrected brief still on the printer. He'd marked it up in the Thursday meeting, loudly, in front of everyone: 'This isn't how we format client briefs.' Now, reading her neat new version, he remembered something uncomfortable. Nobody had ever given her the template. He'd assumed she knew it because he'd known it for three years. He thought of her face in that meeting, very still, eyes on the table. On Monday he stopped by her desk. "About Thursday. The format still needs to be like this; that's not changing. But I pointed it out badly, in front of everyone, and without ever showing you the template. That was on me. Sorry." Fatima looked up, surprised.

qa.q: What had nobody ever given Fatima?
qa.a: Nobody had ever given her the template.

qa.q: What did Mateo feel when he remembered Fatima's still face in the meeting?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising he had been careless with her dignity by assuming she knew the standard.

qa.q: What makes Mateo's apology on Monday a good one?
qa.a: He keeps the correction, since the format still matters, while owning how he said it and the missing template, so the standard stays and her dignity is repaired.

qa.q: What might Fatima be feeling as she looks up, surprised?
qa.a: She may feel relief and fresh respect for Mateo now that he has admitted his part without taking back the feedback.

grounding: A young senior realises he assumed a new colleague knew the standard and embarrassed her, and apologises for the manner while keeping the correction.

passage: After the late-night bulletin, the radio station studio was empty except for Hemant and Vasudha, the programme head. "Parul's script was weak. I'll stand by that," Hemant said, packing his headphones. Vasudha raised an eyebrow. "And how you said it? In the corridor, with guests walking past?" Hemant opened his mouth, then shut it. He remembered Parul's hands shaking as she took the pages back. He'd assumed she knew the station style; he'd never actually shown it to her. The next morning he found Parul at the coffee machine. "Your script still needs cutting to ninety seconds. That part stands. But I shouldn't have said it in the corridor, and I should've given you our style sheet first. I'm sorry." He handed her a printed page.

qa.q: What length does Parul's script still need cutting to?
qa.a: It still needs cutting to ninety seconds.

qa.q: What went through Hemant's mind when he opened his mouth and then shut it?
qa.a: He seemed to realise, uncomfortably, that he had been careless with Parul's dignity and had assumed she knew a style he never shared.

qa.q: How does Hemant manage to apologise without dropping the correction?
qa.a: He repeats that the script must be cut to ninety seconds, then separately owns the public setting and the missing style sheet.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's question have helped Hemant?
qa.a: It nudged him to look at his manner rather than only the content, giving him a chance to reflect before the harm hardened.

grounding: A male senior, prompted by a question, sees he assumed a junior woman knew the standard and embarrassed her, and apologises for the manner but keeps the correction.

passage:
Sangeeta, you asked why I've changed how I run reviews. It's because of an intern called Mehak.
In her second week I tore apart her client summary in the team meeting. "This isn't our format. Did you even look at past reports?" She went red and said nothing.
Then she asked me, very calmly, for a private talk. And she said, "Nobody told me the format. I would have followed it."
I went home and thought about it. She was right. I'd assumed she knew. And I'd been careless with how she felt in front of everyone.
So the next day I told her, "The format still matters, and your summary still needs work. But I said it badly. That was on me." I'm Vinay, and I still think about her red face.

qa.q: What had Vinay said about Mehak's summary in the meeting?
qa.a: "This isn't our format. Did you even look at past reports?"

qa.q: What was Vinay feeling when he went home and thought about it?
qa.a: Vinay felt regretful and uncomfortable, realising the assumption that Mehak knew the format was wrong and that she had been embarrassed publicly.

qa.q: What turning point did Vinay choose, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Vinay apologised for the way the feedback was spoken while keeping the correction, respecting Mehak without lowering the standard.

qa.q: What might Mehak experience when Vinay says "That was on me"?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and respected, knowing the work still needs fixing but her dignity matters too.

grounding: Shows a senior realising he assumed his intern knew the standard and was careless with her dignity, then owning the delivery but not dropping the correction.

passage:
Monday: Baljeet returned Sarika's audit sheet in front of the team. "Wrong columns. Everyone knows this template." Sarika nodded, face tight.
Wednesday: Sarika asked for a private word. She said, calmly, that nobody had shown her the template, and asked if corrections could be private. Baljeet said "Okay" and left. That night, driving home, he replayed Monday. He'd been hired eight years ago. He'd forgotten that nobody is born knowing the template.
Thursday: He stopped at her desk. "The columns still have to be right. That stands. But I shouldn't have said it in front of everyone, and I should have shown you first. Here's the template, with notes."

qa.q: How long ago had Baljeet been hired?
qa.a: Eight years ago.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling as he replayed Monday while driving?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and regretful, realising he had forgotten what it was like to be new.

qa.q: Which part of Baljeet's Thursday message worked well?
qa.a: He kept the correction that the columns must be right, while apologising for the public way he said it and sharing the template.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika to be handed the template with notes?
qa.a: Sarika probably feels relieved and respected, getting both clear standards and an acknowledgement of Monday.

grounding: Shows a senior realising over several days that he assumed the intern knew the template, and owning the delivery while keeping the standard.

passage:
Madhuri, let me tell you about the best boss I ever had. It was 1995. I was your age, a girl of twenty-one, a new trainee at a publishing house, and my boss was Mr Fernandes.
One day he threw my proofread pages on the table in a meeting. "Twenty mistakes! Are you blind?" I wanted the floor to swallow me.
The next morning he called me into his office. He said, "I thought about it. I assumed you'd been taught our style sheet. You weren't. And I spoke to you like you were nothing. That was wrong." Then he handed me back the pages. "The twenty mistakes are still there, mind. Fix them."
I fixed them, beta. And I'd have walked through fire for him after that. That's Vidya's lesson for you.

qa.q: How many mistakes did Mr Fernandes say were on the pages?
qa.a: Twenty mistakes.

qa.q: What might Mr Fernandes have felt when he called Vidya into his office?
qa.a: He likely felt regretful and uncomfortable, having realised he assumed she knew the style sheet and had humiliated her.

qa.q: In the story, what choice did Mr Fernandes make that earned Vidya's loyalty?
qa.a: He owned the harsh way he spoke and his wrong assumption, while still asking her to fix the mistakes.

qa.q: What was young Vidya experiencing in the meeting?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and small, wishing the floor would swallow her after being shouted at in front of others.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boss who realised he had assumed she knew the standard and apologised for his tone while keeping the correction.

passage: The auto had not moved for twenty minutes, stuck behind a broken-down bus on the flyover, and Vikas had nothing to do but think. That morning he had handed back Jaya's cost sheet and said, loud enough for the whole row, "Did nobody teach you to round to two decimals?" She had gone very still. Now he scrolled through his sent emails. Nowhere had he told her the client format. He had simply assumed she knew, the way he knew after six years. The rounding still mattered; the client would reject the sheet. But the way he'd said it. He typed with one thumb while horns blared around him: "Jaya, I was sharp with you this morning, and I'm sorry. The format rule is real, and I never sent it to you. Attaching it now. Can we go through it at ten?"

qa.q: What had Vikas never sent Jaya?
qa.a: He had never told her the client format for the sheet.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling as he sat in the stuck auto?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and regretful, seeing that he had assumed she knew the rule and had embarrassed her in front of the whole row.

qa.q: Why is Vikas's message a good way to repair things?
qa.a: He apologises for his sharp tone but keeps the rounding rule, sends the missing format and offers a time to go through it together.

qa.q: What might Jaya feel when she reads the message?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and respected, learning the mistake came from a rule nobody gave her, not from carelessness.

grounding: Shows a senior realising he assumed the intern knew the standard and was careless with her dignity, then owning his tone while keeping the correction.
